defects: Image does not support a sufficiently distinct teaching answer: The image shows bilateral symmetric MCP-predominant marginal erosions, periarticular osteopenia, soft-tissue swelling, and joint space narrowing — a pattern more consistent with rheumatoid arthritis than psoriatic arthritis mutilans. Psoriatic arthritis mutilans requires pencil-in-cup deformities with preserved or increased bone density and periosteal new bone, which are not clearly demonstrated. The clinical vignette (pitted nails, scaly plaques, telescoping fingers) adds context supporting psoriatic arthritis mutilans, but the radiographic pattern as seen does not show the pathognomonic pencil-in-cup morphology or preserved bone density that would distinguish it from RA. The independent read ranked RA as the primary differential, and no clear discriminating radiographic feature resolves this in favour of psoriatic arthritis mutilans.

findings: Bilateral posteroanterior (PA) projection radiograph of both hands and wrists placed palm-down on the detector
Bilateral symmetrical periarticular soft-tissue swelling most conspicuous at the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) and proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joints
Bilateral symmetrical joint space narrowing at the MCP joints (2nd–5th), more pronounced on the left
Marginal erosions visible at multiple MCP joint heads bilaterally, with loss of normal sharp cortical margins
Periarticular osteopenia most marked around the MCP and PIP joints bilaterally
Carpal bones show mild intercarpal joint space narrowing bilaterally; radiocarpal joint spaces appear relatively preserved
No gross subluxation or dislocation visible on this projection, though early ulnar deviation of fingers cannot be excluded
Soft tissues show generalised swelling without obvious calcification or foreign body
differential: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA): symmetrical MCP-predominant marginal erosions, periarticular osteopenia, soft-tissue swelling, and joint space narrowing in a distribution highly characteristic of RA
Psoriatic arthritis (less likely given apparent periarticular osteopenia and MCP predominance rather than DIP involvement, but cannot be excluded without clinical correlation)
Erosive osteoarthritis (less likely given MCP rather than DIP/PIP predominance and absence of subchondral sclerosis or osteophytes)
anatomyConcerns: The right hand is positioned slightly obliquely compared with the left, causing mild rotation of the carpal bones on that side, which may limit assessment of carpal alignment
Distal forearm and wrist are partially cut off on both sides, limiting full radiocarpal and distal radioulnar joint evaluation
No laterality markers (R/L) or patient identifiers are visible on the image as presented
